documents.abstract: UV–Visible (UV–Vis) spectrophotometry is a rapid, economical and widely available technique for pharmaceutical analysis, but its selectivity is limited when the drugs in a formulation have overlapping absorption spectra. The integration of chemometrics and artificial intelligence (AI), including machine learning (ML) algorithms such as partial least squares (PLS), principal component regression (PCR), support vector regression (SVR), artificial neural networks (ANN) and random forests, with intelligent wavelength selection and metaheuristic optimization (genetic and Firefly algorithms), allows the simultaneous quantification of several active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) from the whole spectrum rather than a single wavelength. This review summarizes the principles of UV–Vis spectroscopy, the current status of AI-assisted UV–Vis analysis, and the challenges related to model interpretability, data integrity, validation and instrument variability. Applications, drawbacks and futureprospects are discussed, including process analytical technology (PAT), portable instruments, green analytical chemistry and regulatory acceptance of AI-enabled spectroscopic methods as complementary tools to chromatographic assays in pharmaceutical quality control.
topics: Spectroscopy Techniques in Biomedical and Chemical Research

documents.abstract: Pharmaceutical marketing is being reshaped by the growing use of digital technologies and artificial intelligence (AI) in communication, customer engagement, and commercial decision-making. Promotion that once relied almost entirely on medical representatives, face-to-face physician visits, product detailing, and printed material is now supplemented, and in some cases reshaped, by digital platforms, social media, e-detailing, webinars, data analytics, and omnichannel communication. This review looks at how AI is being applied to pharmaceutical digital marketing, with particular attention to machine learning, predictive analytics, segmentation of customers and healthcare professionals, personalized communication, customer relationship management, generative AI, and omnichannel engagement. Evidence from the published literature suggests that digital channels widen the reach and flexibility of pharmaceutical communication, while AI adds the ability to analyse large datasets, anticipate behaviour, segment audiences, and personalize content at scale. At the same time, this shift brings its own set of problems: data privacy, inconsistent data quality, algorithmic bias, the risk of misinformation, limited transparency, regulatory compliance, and the continued need for human oversight all surface repeatedly in the literature. Empirical studies also indicate that digital engagement can shape how healthcare professionals are communicated with, influence prescribing-related behaviour, and affect consumer attitudes, though the size of this effect depends heavily on the channel, audience, and therapeutic area involved. Taken together, the evidence points toward a future in which human expertise, digital communication, and AI-supported decision-making work alongside one another rather than one replacing the other. For this model to be sustainable, pharmaceutical marketing will need to be built on responsible implementation, ethical communication, evidence-based content, and clear governance.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) & Machine Learning (ML) are two terms that transformed pharmaceutical sciences, including drug discovery, drug development, precision medicine and nanomedicine. Traditional drug discovery is a long, expensive and failure-prone process that may take over 10 years and million of dollars before it produces a therapeutically active compound ready for clinical trials and commercialization. AI-driven computational approaches can tackle numerous challenges of drug discovery and development, including target or lead identification and optimization, virtual screening, predicting drug target interactions, toxicity and personalized treatment options. The concept of artificial intelligence was first introduced in the 1940s when Alan Turing laid the foundations for machine intelligence theory claiming that there is no fundamental difference between human and machine computation (Turing, 1950). The formal idea of artificial intelligence was further proposed by Mc Carthy, Minsky, Rochester and Shannon who proposed the Dartmouth Hypothesis about the possibility for machines to stimulate human intelligence (Mc Carthy et al 1955). In the following decades the concepts machine learning and deep learning were introduced Schmidhuber in 2015. There are three review papers that discuss the role of AI&ML in pharmaceutical sciences and health care. The first study focus on the role of artificial intelligence in drug discovery and discovery and precision nanomedicine (Zhu et al, 2022). Zhu et al. highlight importance of algorithms and nano-enabled therapeutics for precision nanomedicine. The main ideas of the study include finding and selecting the target developing the optimal drug using nano-enabled therapeutics and individualizing treatment based on patients characteristics. The second review paper discuss the role of AI in spatial structure of protein predicting and drug synergism prediction targeting molecular mechanism and protein drug interactions (Lie et al, 2022). The study by Lei et al. high-light the importance of AI in analyzing and prediction the spatial structure of protein to reveal molecular mechanisms and biological functions. The third review paper was discusses the concept of artificial intelligence, machine learning and deep learning elucidates ethical and social implications and high light the public awarness about AI (Garcia & Salichos, 2022). The study by Garcia & Salichosis a detailed analysis about the opportunities and limitations of AI.I would like to address the main ideas of all three reviewed papers and discuss hoe AL&ML can be applied to various stages of drug discovery and development. I will also comment on such terms as machine learning, deep learning, protein spatial structure prediction, virtual screening precision, precision medicine, nanomedicine, drug synergism prediction, explainable AI.

documents.abstract: Background: Breast cancer is the most frequently diagnosed malignancy in women globally, accounting for approximately 2.30 million new cases and 666,103 deaths in 2022. Artificial intelligence technologies including machine learning, deep learning, radiomics, and natural language processing have been widely applied across the breast cancer care continuum. However, no systematic review restricted to primary studies with patient-level or image-level data has synthesized evidence spanning all clinical domains simultaneously. Objectives: To evaluate the performance, methodological quality, and clinical relevance of artificial intelligence primary studies across screening and diagnostic imaging, digital pathology, radiomics, perioperative management, prognostic prediction, and natural language processing in breast cancer. Methods: PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched from January 2015 to May 2026. Eligibility was restricted to original primary research reporting patient-level or image-level data; secondary syntheses were explicitly excluded. Risk of bias was assessed using QUADAS-2 and PROBAST. Reporting followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Results: Of 5,275 identified records, 17 primary studies met eligibility criteria. In screening mammography (seven studies; n = 7,540 to 144,231 examinations), deep learning achieved area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) values of 0.876 to 0.939; a randomised trial in 80,033 women demonstrated non-inferiority to double reading with a 44.3% reduction in radiologist workload. In digital pathology (five studies; 270 to 44,732 whole-slide images), deep learning achieved AUC 0.985 to 0.994, exceeding unassisted pathologist performance in lymph node metastasis detection. Magnetic resonance imaging radiomics predicted pathological complete response in HER2-positive breast cancer with AUC 0.80. No breast cancer-specific perioperative primary study met the eligibility criteria. Deep survival networks achieved concordance index 0.626 versus 0.612 for Cox regression in breast cancer cohorts. Natural language processing identified metastatic recurrence in breast cancer clinical records with sensitivity 83% and specificity 73%. Risk of bias was low to moderate for imaging and pathology studies and high for small sample radiomics studies. Density-stratified performance was reported by only two imaging studies, and receptor status prediction from haematoxylin and eosin staining had not been validated as a safe alternative to immunohistochemistry. Conclusions: Artificial intelligence demonstrated clinically meaningful performance across the five domains with eligible primary studies. Breast cancer-specific perioperative and intensive care primary studies were absent, representing the largest evidence gap. External validation, demographic diversity, and prospective clinical integration evidence remained the most consistently identified limitations. Prediction of molecular receptor status without immunohistochemistry requires rigorous prospective safety validation before it can complement standard testing.

documents.abstract: Recent digital transformations are redefining the way the financial-accounting ecosystem operates as a result of the integration of ERP (Enterprise Resource Planning) systems and artificial intelligence in accounting, auditing and sustainability reporting processes. As a result of increasing transparency requirements, the adoption of European standards on sustainability reporting and the rapid development of the digital economy, organizations have had to intervene in the process of conducting business, by rethinking operational models and governance mechanisms. The article aims to analyze how the use of ERP systems and artificial intelligence can contribute to the reconfiguration of the financial-accounting ecosystem, facilitating augmented accounting, intelligent auditing and integrated reporting oriented towards economic, environmental and social performance. The objective of the paper is to identify the main opportunities and challenges generated by the integration of ERP systems and artificial intelligence in the financial and accounting activities undertaken by organizations, as well as to highlight the impact on the accounting profession and the decision-making process. The research method used to quantify the key findings relevant to the topic of this article was qualitative, focusing on the responses received from various respondents during interviews conducted with them. The results indicated a high degree of satisfaction of users in the financial-accounting field regarding the generation and analysis of financial and non-financial information, as well as the automation of repetitive activities, the detection of various anomalies and risks, and the monitoring of ESG indicators. The results also highlighted the standardization of data collection processes, the integration of financial and non-financial information into a single platform, the development of digital skills of accounting professionals and auditors, and the promotion of an organizational culture favorable to innovation and change. Thus, the study proposed in this article focuses on providing relevant information for both academia and practitioners or specialists in the financial-accounting and auditing fields regarding the building of intelligent, resilient and sustainable development-oriented organizations.

Purpose: This study aimed to design and evaluate an artificial intelligence–based model for predicting the mathematics performance of twelfth-grade experimental sciences students based on individual, educational, and learning technology factors. Methods and Materials: This applied, quantitative, cross-sectional, and predictive study was conducted among twelfth-grade experimental sciences students in Isfahan, Iran. A total of 187 questionnaires were distributed, and after removing incomplete, inconsistent, and invalid records, data from 84 students were retained for analysis. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire assessing individual factors, educational conditions, and learning technology variables, together with students’ recorded mathematics scores. The dataset was divided into training and testing subsets, and repeated five-fold cross-validation was used for internal model development. Multiple linear regression, ridge regression, lasso regression, elastic net regression, decision tree regression, random forest regression, gradient boosting regression, and support vector regression were compared. Model performance was evaluated using mean absolute error, root mean squared error, and the coefficient of determination. Findings: Previous mathematics achievement had the strongest positive correlation with current mathematics performance, followed by mathematics self-efficacy, study regularity, academic motivation, teacher feedback, instructional quality, and educational use of learning technologies. Test anxiety and digital distraction were negatively associated with mathematics performance. Among the evaluated algorithms, gradient boosting regression achieved the best predictive performance, with a test-set mean absolute error of 0.93, root mean squared error of 1.26, and coefficient of determination of .72. Previous mathematics achievement, mathematics self-efficacy, study regularity, teacher feedback, educational use of learning technologies, test anxiety, and instructional quality were the most influential predictors. Adding educational factors increased explained variance from .54 to .65, while including learning technology factors further increased it to .72. Conclusion: The findings indicate that mathematics performance can be predicted with acceptable accuracy by integrating students’ prior achievement, psychological and behavioral characteristics, instructional experiences, and learning technology use within an interpretable artificial intelligence model.

Purpose: This study aimed to design an artificial intelligence–based cognitive empowerment package for enhancing entrepreneurial skills in gifted and creative adolescents through the qualitative identification and integration of relevant cognitive, psychological, motivational, interpersonal, and technological components. Methods and Materials: The study employed a qualitative exploratory-developmental design. Data were obtained through an analytical review of relevant literature, examination of previous student entrepreneurship workshop experiences, and semi-structured interviews with students, mentors, workshop facilitators, and accelerator managers selected through purposive sampling. Data collection continued until conceptual saturation was achieved. Interview transcripts, field observations, documentary evidence, and analytical notes were examined using thematic analysis. Findings: The qualitative analysis indicated that sustained entrepreneurial action among gifted and creative adolescents depends on a multidimensional configuration of entrepreneurial intention and identity, self-efficacy, opportunity recognition and problem identification, executive functioning, tolerance of ambiguity, applied creativity, fear of failure and perfectionism, intrinsic motivation and psychological ownership, teamwork and psychological safety, proactive agency, resilience, future orientation, and reflective readiness to use artificial intelligence. The findings further suggested that entrepreneurial difficulties differ across adolescents and therefore require profile-based rather than uniform intervention. Integration of the themes resulted in a six-session package encompassing profile awareness and goal setting, problem identification and value creation, conversion of ideas into action plans, presentation and feedback utilization, teamwork and agency, and final presentation with a continuation plan. Conclusion: The findings suggest that entrepreneurial empowerment in gifted and creative adolescents should extend beyond creativity and business knowledge by strengthening the cognitive and psychological capacities required to transform ideas into sustained action, while using artificial intelligence as a supervised reflective and personalized learning support rather than as a substitute for adolescent judgment and agency.

The primary objective of the present study was to design and explain an entrepreneurship model for artificial intelligence–based businesses, with a focus on the information and communications technology and computer software industries in knowledge-based companies located in Tehran Province. In terms of purpose, the study was applied, and in terms of approach, it was a qualitative study employing a sequential exploratory design. In the qualitative phase, grounded theory was applied using the systematic approach to identify and conceptualize the dimensions, components, and relationships among the variables affecting AI-based entrepreneurship. The qualitative research field consisted of senior and middle managers, specialists, experts, and experienced employees working in the information and communications technology and computer software industries of knowledge-based companies in Tehran Province. Participants were selected through purposive sampling, which continued until theoretical saturation was reached. Qualitative data were collected through semi-structured interviews and analyzed using MAXQDA 2024. To enhance the credibility and trustworthiness of the data, triangulation and Lincoln and Guba’s criteria, including credibility, transferability, dependability, and confirmability, were employed. The findings indicated that the entrepreneurship model for AI-based businesses consists of an interconnected set of causal conditions, contextual conditions, intervening conditions, strategies, and consequences. The causal conditions included factors such as market needs and technological gaps, entrepreneurial opportunity recognition, and customers’ digital preferences, all of which played a fundamental role in the formation of AI-based entrepreneurship. The contextual conditions included the need to establish a knowledge-based ecosystem, policymaking and regulations, financial capabilities and initial investment, advanced technological capacities, specialized human capital, team competencies, and intraorganizational collaboration. Intervening conditions, including legal and regulatory constraints associated with sensitive data and cybersecurity, as well as economic restrictions and sanctions, were also found to affect the development of entrepreneurship. According to the findings, the key strategies were the development of strategic collaborations, product development and upgrading, digital marketing and market penetration, and human capital empowerment. Finally, the consequences of implementing the model included economic and financial maturity, the development of technological authority, social and employment effects, digital transformation in upstream industries, and software export development.

The digital transformation has reshaped entrepreneurship, with the emergence of artificial intelligence (AI) as a powerful enabler of innovation and startup creation. However, higher education institutions face challenges integrating AI into entrepreneurship education curriculum, limiting students’ ability to fully harness its potential. This study aimed to determine and explore entrepreneurship students’ challenges in using AI for startup development, assess the competencies they gain in innovating business ideas, and analyze how these challenges affect competencies using structural equation modeling (SEM). Employing an convergent mixed-method design, the study surveyed 114 third- and fourth-year BS Entrepreneurship students and conducted interviews to faculty and business plan implementers. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and SEM, while qualitative data underwent thematic analysis for triangulation. Findings revealed that students face significant challenges in opportunity identification, decision-making, performance execution, education and learning, and research application. The key barriers highlight was market understanding, lack of AI literacy, limited mentorship, and insufficient curriculum integration. Despite these, students reported gaining competencies in opportunity recognition, customer targeting, data-informed decision-making, and entrepreneurial communication using AI tools. However, critical thinking, problem-solving, and prototyping skills remained underdeveloped. SEM results indicated that challenges in education, opportunity identification, and decision-making significantly constrained entrepreneurial competencies. The study implies the need for higher education to reform curricula by embedding AI-focused modules, case-based projects, mentorship opportunities, and innovation hubs. Strengthening AI-driven entrepreneurship education will equip students with the competencies required for sustainable startup creation in the digital economy.

In recent years, the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in research involving human participants has gained popularity in clinical and biomedical research domains, more so in advance economies than in low medium income countries (LMIC) like Cameroon. AI is transformative in its ability to perform faster repetitive tasks, analyze large amounts of data, and potentially leading to enhance clinical research decision-making. As with all research involving human participants, research using AI should be in compliance with ethical principles and subject to regulatory guidelines for better protection of volunteering research participants. The use of AI in research involving human participants presents new ethical and regulatory challenges, including those related to privacy and data confidentiality, transparency, amplification of bias, and implications for maintaining human autonomy and oversight. Existing guidelines of most research ethics committees relating to digital health technology evaluation for human research are not up-to- date to address AI evaluation in clinical research. In view of providing a regulatory compliant structure that protects the human participant’s privacy and mitigation of bias Sub-Saharan African countries have an obligation to update their standard operating procedures to integrate aspects for evaluating AI research. There are however, a few existing guidelines from developed countries like the US and Canada that provide the ethical foundations for the use of AI in clinical research. Tools are still required to enhance the protocol review process by the research ethics committees charged with ensuring consistency, efficiency and sustainability across institutions, to reflect accepted standards of ethical research review oversight. This document aims to focus on AI contributions in clinical research, challenges and adopted guidelines for evaluation of AI-driven clinical research. This is in view of providing support for Institutional Review Boards (IRBs) and other ethics advocacy institutions with the awareness and practical friendly user steps to identify, assess, and mitigate potential risks to participants in an AI-driven research, during the ethical review process.

documents.abstract: Traditional medicine systems continue to serve as primary healthcare resources for a substantial proportion of the global population, particularly in low- and middle-income countries where access to modern medical infrastructure remains limited. Ethnopharmacology has emerged as a critical interdisciplinary field that systematically bridges indigenous knowledge systems with contemporary biomedical science, enabling scientific validation, standardization, and integration of traditional therapeutic practices. This comprehensive review examines the evolving role of ethnopharmacology in advancing holistic treatment paradigms through methodological innovations such as network pharmacology, systems biology, metabolomics, artificial intelligence, and multi-omics technologies. The paper critically analyzes multimodal therapeutic strategies, constitutional typing frameworks, and mind–body integration approaches embedded within traditional medicine systems. Furthermore, it evaluates current challenges related to clinical validation, quality control, regulatory harmonization, safety assessment, and ethical issues including intellectual property rights and equitable benefit-sharing. Emerging evidence suggests that traditional medicine offers promising complementary strategies for managing complex chronic and multifactorial diseases; however, rigorous interdisciplinary research, robust clinical methodologies, and culturally sensitive policy frameworks are essential for its sustainable integration into global healthcare systems. Strengthening collaborations between traditional knowledge holders and scientific communities will be pivotal in developing equitable, evidence-based, and patient-centered holistic healthcare models.

The rapid integration of artificial intelligence into biomedical research and clinical practice is transforming the ways in which the human body is conceptualized and represented in medical knowledge. Rather than functioning merely as descriptive tools, scientific vocabularies and research frameworks contribute to shaping epistemic models of the body. This study investigates how contemporary medical literature reproduces particular representations of the body in the context of digital medicine and artificial intelligence. Methodologically, the research combines bibliometric mapping with discourse analysis. A systematic search of the PubMed database identified 2,518 articles published between 1973 and 2025 that include references to the body and artificial intelligence. From these articles, 7,275 keywords were extracted and analysed, with 499 terms meeting the minimum occurrence threshold for co-occurrence mapping using VOSviewer. The bibliometric analysis reveals the centrality of technical concepts associated with computational modelling, including neural networks, image processing, and computational biology. Complementary discourse analysis of the articles indicates that the body is predominantly conceptualized as a biomechanical structure, an imaging object, a network of physiological sensors, or a dataset analysed through predictive algorithms. In contrast, experiential and narrative dimensions of embodiment appear significantly less visible within the dominant vocabulary of biomedical research. Based on these findings, the study proposes a conceptual model of the digital body, describing the transformation of the body from a clinically observed organism into a data-driven object embedded within technological infrastructures of monitoring, modelling, and prediction. The analysis suggests that while digital medicine expands the technological capacities of healthcare, it also risks narrowing the conceptual space in which the body is understood. In this context, the integration of perspectives from medical humanities becomes increasingly important for reconnecting biomedical innovation with the lived, ethical, and narrative dimensions of human embodiment.

documents.abstract: The present study was conducted with the aim of identifying and validating the components affecting the sustainability of the banking network, using both qualitative and quantitative phases. In the qualitative phase, a meta-synthesis approach was employed, and based on a systematic search of reputable scientific databases, 79 articles were identified. After applying the inclusion and exclusion criteria, 16 selected studies were analyzed. The findings of this phase indicated that in the economic and financial dimension, components such as operational efficiency and sustainable profitability, credit and liquidity risk management, capital adequacy and balance sheet structure, exposure to foreign exchange risk, and asset quality play a significant role in banking stability. In the institutional and corporate governance dimension, ownership structure, effective supervisory systems, and macroeconomic conditions were identified as key factors. In the technological dimension, components such as digital transformation, development of modern banking infrastructure, cybersecurity, and the use of artificial intelligence for risk management were found to be of particular importance. In the social dimension, banks’ social responsibility, transparency in communications, and enhancement of customer experience were identified as influential factors affecting public trust and social capital. In the quantitative phase, confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) was employed to validate the components extracted from the qualitative analysis. The results indicate that the sustainability of the banking network requires an integrated approach that simultaneously strengthens the economic, institutional, technological, and social dimensions.

The present study aimed to identify the key factors and strategic drivers affecting sustainable auditing within the framework of sustainability reporting. This applied research was conducted using a descriptive-survey methodology with a futures studies approach. The study employed a paradigmatic qualitative model as the foundation for hypothesis development and cause-and-effect analysis. Data were collected using a researcher-made questionnaire distributed through block random sampling among experts and specialists in auditing, accounting, and futures studies. The cross-impact analysis method (MICMAC) was applied to analyze the relationships among variables and identify influential and dependent components. An 8×8 matrix was completed by six experts who evaluated the degree of influence among variables using a four-point scale ranging from no impact to strong impact. The research process also incorporated Delphi rounds and scenario analysis to identify possible future states of sustainable auditing. The findings demonstrated that uncertainty, social trust, and auditor independence were classified as linkage and risk variables with high influence and dependence, while technology emerged as the strongest influential variable in the system. Stakeholder pressure was identified as an autonomous variable, whereas institutional challenge, auditor role, and sustainability linkage were classified as dependent variables. MICMAC analysis revealed a matrix fill rate of 87.5%, indicating a highly interconnected system among the identified components. Strategic variables affecting the future of sustainable auditing included technology, uncertainty, social trust, and auditor independence. Furthermore, four future scenarios were extracted: symbolic auditing, trust-regulating institution, reactive-minimal auditing, and predictive and strategic auditing. The results indicated that the future evolution of sustainable auditing depends significantly on technological advancement, regulatory maturity, professional competencies, stakeholder pressure, and the intelligent use of artificial intelligence and ESG-based analytical systems. The study concluded that sustainable auditing is evolving from a traditional compliance-oriented activity toward a future-oriented institutional mechanism for trust creation and strategic governance. The integration of technology, sustainability legitimacy, auditor independence, and uncertainty management plays a critical role in shaping the effectiveness of sustainable auditing systems. The proposed framework provides a comprehensive basis for policymakers, regulators, and professional auditing bodies to improve sustainability assurance practices and strengthen organizational accountability in response to environmental, social, and governance challenges.

Toxicity remains a major consideration in drug discovery because a compound must combine therapeutic activity with an acceptable safety profile. Conventional toxicity testing provides essential biological evidence but can be resource-intensive and may be difficult to apply to large chemical libraries at an early stage. In silico toxicity screening provides a complementary, data-driven approach for identifying potential safety liabilities before extensive experimental testing. This review summarises the transition from conventional toxicology to digital toxicology and discusses quantitative structure–activity relationship (QSAR) modelling, read-across, molecular docking, toxicokinetic modelling, machine learning, deep learning and artificial intelligence (AI) approaches. Major toxicity endpoints, including cardiotoxicity, hepatotoxicity, nephrotoxicity, neurotoxicity, genotoxicity, carcinogenicity, reproductive and developmental toxicity, immunotoxicity and respiratory toxicity, are considered from a computational perspective. The article also examines how computational methods can support ADMET profiling, lead optimisation, candidate prioritisation and early toxicity-based deprioritisation. Although digital methods can improve speed, scalability and consistency, their reliability depends on data quality, model validation, applicability domain, interpretability and experimental confirmation. Future toxicology is expected to increasingly integrate AI, multi-omics, human-relevant in vitro systems, organ-on-chip models and New Approach Methodologies (NAMs). Overall, computational toxicity assessment is best viewed as a complementary component of an integrated safety strategy rather than a replacement for experimental toxicology.

The most exciting development in nanomedicine is the injectable nanorobots that combine nanotechnology, robotics, biotechnology, materials science, and artificial intelligence for extremely accurate illness detection and treatment. In contrast to conventional drug delivery systems that disperse medication throughout the body, injectable nanorobots are engineered to navigate bodily fluids, detect disease-specific biomarkers, and release therapeutic agents selectively at the target site. These systems have demonstrated significant potential in areas such as cancer, cardiovascular disease, neurological conditions, infectious diseases, regenerative medicine, and precision diagnostics. Recent advancements in enzyme-powered, magnetic, ultrasound-driven, and biohybrid nanorobots have expedited the transfer of these technologies from lab research to preclinical and early translational investigations. Biocompatibility, biodegradability, large-scale production, real-time navigation, regulatory approval, and long-term biosafety are some of the issues that still need to be resolved despite the tremendous advancements. The present understanding of injectable nanorobots, including their historical evolution, classification, structural elements, fabrication techniques, propulsion mechanisms, targeting tactics, biological applications, safety issues, and potential future clinical uses, is compiled in this review. A thorough overview of this quickly developing topic discusses recent developments and new trends.

SignificanceIn recent years, the rapid advancement of industrial digitalization and intelligentization has extended the boundaries of cyberspace into the physical world, and urban rail transit systems, as critical national information infrastructure, have been exposed to increasingly severe cybersecurity threats. The network environment of urban rail industrial control systems is characterized by wide-area deployment, dynamic evolution, and strong heterogeneity. Extensive network coverage, dynamically changing operating conditions, and diverse equipment types and communication protocols impose higher requirements on the timeliness, accuracy, adaptability, and coordination capabilities of cybersecurity defenses. Conventional cybersecurity defenses often lack sufficient awareness and remain reactive in these environments, making timely and accurate discovery and identification of wide-area network threats difficult. Static and passive protection mechanisms cannot be readily adjusted to changes in network conditions and threats, while unified management and coordination of heterogeneous cybersecurity devices remain insufficient. Consequently, limited accuracy and timeliness in threat monitoring, static and passive defense mechanisms, and weak unified management and coordination capabilities remain major technical challenges. These challenges are further complicated by the interconnection of control centers, stations, train networks, and cloud platforms, through which threats may be propagated across different operational domains. Meanwhile, strict requirements for train operation safety, real-time control, and service continuity must be satisfied during security monitoring and defensive operations. Timely threat discovery must therefore be reconciled with accurate identification, and defensive policies must be adapted to changing network conditions and threat patterns. Research on artificial immunity and large language models is consequently needed to support the recognition of unfamiliar threats, the dynamic optimization of defensive policies, and the coordinated management of heterogeneous cybersecurity devices.ProgressTo address these challenges, artificial immunity and large language models were incorporated into a research framework for complex urban rail industrial control networks. Timely and accurate wide-area threat discovery, proactive defense against dynamically evolving threats, and collaborative orchestration of heterogeneous cybersecurity devices were identified as the three principal research problems. Three core techniques together with an integrated prototype system were included in the proposed framework. Specifically, an artificial-immune-recognition-based risk monitoring method was proposed to enable rapid threat detection and precise identification. Multisource heterogeneous data were considered for feature fusion and representation in a unified immune feature space. Traffic, logs, alerts, protocol commands, and equipment states were included among the information sources. Hierarchical clustering and detector tolerance training were incorporated into the detector generation scheme, and rapid responses within detector clusters were proposed to improve monitoring efficiency. A dual-verification mechanism was introduced, in which preliminary screening with self detectors was followed by further identification with non-self detectors. An artificial-immune-evolution-based proactive defense framework was then proposed to enhance protection against persistent and multistage attacks. Clonal proliferation and hierarchical differential evolution were incorporated into threat gene evolution to support the exploration of potential threat patterns. Stochastic attack-defense games and deep learning were combined in the proposed technical route for defense policy generation and adaptive dynamic optimization. Successive states, available actions, immediate rewards and costs, and expected future returns were considered in the game-based modeling of attack-defense interactions. A large-language-model-based collaborative management approach was also presented to coordinate diverse security devices for joint defense. Heterogeneous threat intelligence was organized within a cloud-edge-endpoint architecture for collection, aggregation, compression, and storage. The knowledge reasoning and generation capabilities of large language models were incorporated into intelligence analysis and the generation of cross-domain coordination plans. Risk monitoring systems, proactive defense systems, firewalls, and cryptographic appliances were included among the intended managed devices. Policy consistency checks, coordinated distribution, execution verification, and audit records were incorporated into the system design. Building upon this foundation, a prototype intelligent cybersecurity defense architecture was presented for urban rail transit systems, and system integration, deployment arrangements, and technical validation were outlined.Conclusions and ProspectsAn integrated research framework was proposed for cybersecurity defense in urban rail transit systems, with risk monitoring, proactive defense, and coordinated device management connected through three complementary technical directions. Artificial immune recognition was introduced for timely threat discovery and accurate identification, immune evolution was incorporated into adaptive defense policy generation, and large language models were introduced for heterogeneous threat intelligence analysis and collaborative device management. A technical route beyond traditional patch-based passive defense was thereby outlined to support the secure and reliable operation of national critical information infrastructure. Further research should be directed toward the adaptation of these techniques to actual urban rail operating conditions. Dynamic self-boundary modeling and unknown-threat recognition should be refined in response to changes in operating schedules, equipment conditions, and maintenance activities. Defense policy generation and optimization should be investigated under the constraints of train operation safety, real-time control, and service continuity. The explainability and traceability of generated management plans, cross-device policy consistency, and coordinated execution should also be strengthened. Prototype integration should be advanced, followed by system simulation, attack-defense evaluation, and third-party performance testing. Threat detection accuracy, response latency, dynamic defense policy generation, and coordinated handling across multiple devices should be evaluated, and application feedback should be used to refine the proposed technologies and methods.

Long-acting injectables (LAIs) are innovative drug-delivery systems allowing for prolonged controlled release of a drug after a single administration. By decreasing the dosing frequency, long-acting injectable can have a positive impact on treatment compliance, patient convenience, and drug exposure while minimising the peak–trough fluctuations. This review provides an overview of the different formulation approaches used to develop LAIs, including microspheres, Nano crystal suspensions, oil-based depots, in situ forming depots, implants, hydrogels, lyotropic liquid crystalline systems, polymer-lipid hybrids, and modified protein and peptide therapeutics. The review highlights the main advantages and limitations of LAIs, such as patient adherence and consistent drug exposure, while also discussing injection site reactions, prolonged drug exposure, challenges of flexible dose adjustment, manufacturing complexity, and cost. Storage requirements will be discussed. The clinical applications in schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, HIV treatment and prevention, opioid use disorder, growth hormone deficiency, and diabetes. Ophthalmic diseases will be highlighted together with the marketed products in each therapeutic area. Finally, emerging technologies, patient-friendly LAI approaches, biomaterials, artificial intelligence, predictive modelling, and personalised medicine are discussed. In conclusion, LAIs are an important class of drug delivery systems that can have a significant impact on optimal and sustained drug exposure while decreasing the treatment burden on the patient. The complexity of the different formulation approaches and the need for clinical development expertise are still major hurdles that industry is currently trying to address by developing new approaches and manufacturing processes.

Benefiting from recent advances in generative AI and large language models (LLMs), current LLM-driven AI systems are rapidly reshaping how we reason, plan, and make decisions. Yet endowing these systems with human-like temporal intelligence (e.g., understanding and comparing events across time) remains largely unresolved. To address this gap, we introduce a novel Multi-dimensional Hierarchical Temporal Alignment framework (denoted as MHTA), of which the core idea is to effectively ground the temporal alignment of an LLM in both event-specific and cross-event real-world temporal commonsense knowledge. Specifically, we first frame the temporal space as a multi-dimensional hierarchical space, where each dimension comprises its own set of temporal units. Building on this formulation, we curate an initial burn-in dataset in which annotations are constructed to reflect real-world human temporal commonsense in accordance with our defined temporal space. Based on the initial burn-in dataset, we propose two complementary fine-tuning objectives: (i) Grounding the temporal alignment in event-specific temporal commonsense knowledge, which is achieved through a novel hierarchy-preserving Wasserstein loss, and (ii) Grounding the temporal alignment in cross-event temporal commonsense knowledge, which is achieved via a margin-adaptive triplet loss. To evaluate the effectiveness of MHTA, we conduct extensive experiments on three representative benchmarks (MCTACO, DurationQA, and TimeDial). For example, on the MCTACO dataset, MHTA improves Mistral-7B by 6.0% in accuracy and 10.3% in exact match, and improves DeepSeek-LLM-7B by 5.4% in accuracy and 9.8% in exact match. Combined with different backbones, MHTA surpasses nearly all baselines across the three benchmarks and exceeds the performance of advanced models such as GPT-4o on MCTACO and DurationQA. These results demonstrate that MHTA provides consistent gains in temporal commonsense reasoning across diverse LLM backbones.

Transdermal drug delivery systems (TDDS) provide several advantages over conventional oral and parenteral routes, including avoidance of gastrointestinal degradation and hepatic first-pass metabolism, improved patient compliance, and controlled drug delivery. However, the stratum corneum acts as a major barrier, limiting the passive transport of hydrophilic and high-molecular-weight therapeutic agents. This review focuses on recent advances in polymeric microneedles and nanocarrier-mediated transdermal drug delivery systems developed to overcome these skin-permeation limitations. Literature from PubMed and Scopus was reviewed with emphasis on microneedle classification, polymeric biomaterials, nanocarrier systems, drug-loading capacity, permeation mechanisms, safety, and clinical translation. Polymeric microneedles, including solid, coated, dissolving, hydrogel-forming, and hollow systems, enable controlled and minimally painful delivery by creating temporary microchannels through the stratum corneum. Nanocarriers such as liposomes, ethosomes, solid lipid nanoparticles, nanostructured lipid carriers, polymeric nanoparticles, and inorganic nanoparticles further enhance dermal and transdermal drug transport through lipid fluidization, follicular pathways, and controlled drug deposition. The integration of these technologies provides promising opportunities for delivering macromolecules, vaccines, and localized therapeutics. Future developments involving stimuli-responsive systems, wearable biosensors, artificial intelligence, microfluidics, and personalized manufacturing may further enhance transdermal therapy. Despite challenges related to manufacturing scalability, regulatory standardization, and long-term biocompatibility, advanced microneedle and nanocarrier platforms have considerable potential for clinical translation and personalized drug delivery. Background: Traditional transdermal drug delivery systems (TDDS) provide a non-invasive, patient-compliant route that avoids gastrointestinal degradation and hepatic first-pass metabolism. However, the impermeable lipid matrix of the stratum corneum strictly limits the passive transport of molecules to those possessing specific hydrophobic profiles and low molecular weights. Objective: This comprehensive review examines contemporary physical and chemical breakthrough technologies, with specific focus on polymeric microneedles (MNs) and nanocarrier-facilitated delivery platforms engineered to overcome these macro-molecular transport constraints. Methodology: A systematic screening of literature from the PubMed and Scopus databases (spanning foundational models through 2026) was conducted to evaluate the mechanical structural properties, biopolymer selections, and systemic pharmacokinetics of advanced skin-permeation platforms. Results: Polymeric microneedles (dissolving, hydrogel-forming, and stimuli-responsive types) demonstrate precise disruption of the stratum corneum without contacting dermally located pain-sensitive nerve endings. Concurrently, lipidic, polymeric, and inorganic nanocarriers capitalize on hair follicles and transient lipid fluidization to deposit high-molecular-weight biologics, vaccines, and localized therapeutics. Conclusion: Combining active mechanical microneedles with target-specific nanocarriers represents the vanguard of modern personalized diagnostics and therapeutics, bridging laboratory innovation with clinical scale-up paradigms.

Driver Monitoring Systems (DMS) are becoming increasingly integrated within modern vehicles, driven by advances in sensing technologies, artificial intelligence and evolving regulatory requirements. While previous research has largely focused on drivers’ perceptions and system performance, comparatively little attention has been given to the perspectives of the stakeholders who design, develop, regulate and implement these technologies. This study explored expert stakeholder views on the current role, challenges and future direction of DMS in the UK automotive sector. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with seven stakeholders representing vehicle manufacturers, applied research institutions, safety and regulatory experts, technology developers and testing organisations, and user experience (UX) design experts. Data were analysed using inductive thematic analysis. Six themes emerged: (1) DMS as a compliance-driven system; (2) misalignment with drivers’ mental models; (3) lack of personalisation; (4) intrusiveness and annoyance; (5) trust and acceptance; and (6) DMS as part of a broader socio-technical system. Stakeholders consistently viewed current DMS implementations as being driven primarily by regulatory compliance rather than user needs, with concerns that rigid thresholds, poorly calibrated alerts and limited transparency undermine driver trust and encourage system disengagement or misuse. Participants emphasised the importance of adaptive, context-aware and human-centred approaches to design that better accommodate individual differences while balancing privacy, usability and regulatory requirements. The findings demonstrate that the effectiveness of DMS depends not only on sensing performance but also on how systems interact with drivers within a wider socio-technical context. The study provides an expert stakeholder perspective that complements existing driver-focused research and identifies key priorities for future human factors research, including adaptive monitoring, improved human-machine interaction, regulatory evaluation and ethical governance. These findings offer practical insights for researchers, manufacturers and policymakers seeking to support the safe and acceptable deployment of next-generation driver monitoring technologies.

Much foundational work in Sociology of Law (SoL) has considered the role of law in society as well as the role of society in law. This duality has opened for nuanced accounts of the impact of formal law (referred as legal norms herein) by empirically studying formal laws and everyday interactions making up various social norms which may at times align with one another or be in conflict. Recently, technological elements, as part of social structures, have been addressed in terms of socio-legal relevancy of digitalisation (Hydén [2022]) and artificial intelligence (AI) (Larsson [2019]) and formal law. In this entry, we address a specific subset of technologies in need of more socio-legal scrutiny as this phenomenon is likely to be of greater importance in the near future: social robots.

This article presents an autoethnographic account of teaching first-year digital communication in an AI-saturated classroom. It examines how the widespread use of generative AI tools has transformed students’ relationship to learning, leading to the progressive outsourcing of cognitive tasks such as writing, analysis, and argumentation. Drawing on classroom observations across multiple cohorts, the study identifies a pattern of declining student engagement, reduced motivation for skill development, and a widening gap between AI-assisted outputs and students’ independent abilities. It conceptualizes this process as competence atrophy, reinforced by a feedback loop of dependency and by institutional structures that prioritize efficiency and output over learning processes. The article also reflects on the changing role of the teaching assistant, the challenges of assessing authentic competence, and the broader implications for higher education. It concludes by proposing pedagogical strategies centered on process-based assessment, intellectual ownership, and the revaluation of learning as an intrinsically meaningful activity.

Artificial intelligence is increasingly embedded within the decision architectures of contemporary organizations. AI systems classify information, rank alternatives, generate recommendations, prioritize cases, allocate resources, identify risks, constrain options, and increasingly execute organizational actions. These capabilities are commonly examined through automation, human oversight, accountability, and responsible-AI lenses. They also raise a more foundational governance question: where does institutional authority reside when algorithmic systems materially shape organizational outcomes? This issue of The Intelligent Enterprise Review introduces the Algorithmic Authority Imperative as an enterprise-governance perspective concerned with the distribution, migration, constraint, accountability, and reversibility of institutional authority in AI-enabled organizations. It defines Algorithmic Authority as the capacity of an AI system to materially shape, constrain, prioritize, recommend, determine, or execute institutional outcomes through its position within an organization's decision architecture. The manuscript distinguishes Formal Authority from Functional Authority and develops Authority Migration to describe the movement of substantive institutional influence or decision power from established human roles or governance structures toward technological systems, including circumstances in which no explicit organizational decision to transfer equivalent authority has occurred. Related constructs include De Facto Algorithmic Authority, Authority Creep, the Authority–Accountability Gap, Authority Capability Decay, Institutional Entrenchment, Algorithmic Authority Boundaries, and Authority Reversibility. These concepts are integrated through the Algorithmic Authority Doctrine™ and the Algorithmic Authority Governance Framework™, organized around six enterprise capabilities: Authority Visibility, Authority Boundaries, Decision Rights, Challenge Capacity, Accountability Alignment, and Authority Reversibility. The central proposition is that effective AI governance requires organizations to govern not only what artificial intelligence can do, but also the institutional authority that accumulates around its use. Consequential algorithmic authority should remain visible, legitimate, bounded, reviewable, challengeable, accountable, and reversible. The issue extends The Intelligent Enterprise Review's broader intellectual architecture connecting Decision Sovereignty, Judgment Sovereignty, Algorithmic Authority Governance, and Institutional Durability in the design of the governed intelligent enterprise.

documents.abstract: Starting in the 2025/2026 academic year, Coding and Artificial Intelligence (Koding dan Kecerdasan Artifisial, KKA) was introduced as an elective subject from grade five in Indonesian elementary schools. This quasi-experimental study compared a KKA module based on Pembelajaran Mendalam (mindful, meaningful, and joyful learning)—a pedagogical approach distinct from machine-learning-based deep learning—with application-only instruction. Sixty-five fifth-grade students from two schools in South Tangerang participated (experimental n = 33; control n = 32). Across six 70-minute meetings, the module integrated unplugged activities, Scratch, a simple image-classification tool, and reflection. Computational thinking tests, a learning-experience questionnaire, and observations supplied the data. Posttest mean scores were 76.88 (experimental) and 65.40 (control), t(63) = 4.73, p < .001, d = 1.17; corresponding N-gains were 0.58 and 0.37. Descriptively, the largest indicator gain in the experimental group was decomposition (0.62), while the smallest was abstraction (0.47). In this two-school sample, the module was associated with greater computational-thinking gains than application-only instruction; the design does not establish which component produced the difference.

Objective: The present study aimed to investigate the effect of artificial intelligence–induced stress on employees’ individual creativity, considering the mediating role of stress-coping strategies and the moderating role of management commitment. Methods and Materials: In terms of purpose, this was an applied study, and methodologically, it employed a descriptive survey design. The statistical population comprised all permanent employees of the Yazd City Gas Company between September 2025 and March 2026. Based on Cochran’s formula, 125 employees were selected through simple random sampling. Data were collected using the standardized questionnaire developed by Tong et al. (2025), which assessed artificial intelligence–induced stress, stress-coping strategies, individual creativity, and management commitment. The validity of the instrument was confirmed through confirmatory factor analysis, average variance extracted, and the Fornell–Larcker criterion, while its reliability was verified using Cronbach’s alpha and composite reliability. The data were analyzed using SPSS version 26 and structural equation modeling in SmartPLS version 4. Findings: The results indicated that artificial intelligence–induced stress had a direct and significant effect on stress-coping strategies, which, in turn, significantly enhanced employees’ individual creativity. The indirect effect of artificial intelligence–induced stress on individual creativity through the mediating variable of stress-coping strategies was also confirmed. However, the direct effect of artificial intelligence–induced stress on individual creativity was not statistically significant. Furthermore, the moderating role of management commitment in the relationship between artificial intelligence–induced stress and stress-coping strategies was not confirmed. Conclusion: The findings demonstrated that artificial intelligence–induced stress does not necessarily lead directly to a reduction in employee creativity; rather, the manner in which employees manage and cope with this stress determines its creative outcomes. The use of adaptive coping strategies can transform technology-related pressures into opportunities for learning, intrinsic motivation, and creative ideation.

Rapid technological developments have enabled the world of education to benefit, one of which is the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in learning practices. Simultaneously, the Kurikulum Merdeka, which prioritizes flexibility in learning methods, has also undergone development, including the inclusion of AI and coding as elective subjects. Teachers, as educators who prepare teaching materials and learning methods for students, need to adapt to these changes. This study analyzes the effectiveness and challenges of implementing the Kurikulum Merdeka, which incorporates AI subjects through a Deep Learning (Pembelajaran Mendalam or PM) approach in accounting instruction. The study used a descriptive qualitative method, including semi-structured interviews, observations, and document analysis, with the vice principal for curriculum, accounting teachers, and library managers. The results showed positive impacts, including increased student participation, deeper conceptual understanding, and practical skills aligned with industry needs. However, several challenges remain that hinder implementation, including rapid policy changes, inadequate teaching materials, teacher preparedness, and a lack of supporting resources, such as up-to-date textbooks. To ensure optimal implementation, teacher competency development, comprehensive teaching materials, policy consistency, and collaboration between schools and libraries are needed for sustained effectiveness. Abstrak Perkembangan teknologi yang semakin pesat memungkinkan dunia pendidikan turut merasakan manfaatnya, salah satunya adalah penggunaan Artificial Intelligence (AI) dalam praktik pembelajaran. Bersamaan dengan itu, Kurikulum Merdeka yang mengutamakan fleksibilitas dalam metode belajar juga mengalami perkembangan, salah satunya adalah dengan masuknya pilihan mata pelajaran AI dan coding dalam kurikulum. Guru sebagai pendidik yang mempersiapkan bahan ajar dan metode belajar kepada murid perlu menyesuaikan diri pada perubahan tersebut. Penelitian ini menganalisis efektivitas dan tantangan implementasi Kurikulum Merdeka dengan masuknya mata pelajaran AI melalui pendekatan Pembelajaran Mendalam (PM) dalam pembelajaran akuntansi. Penelitian menggunakan metode kualitatif deskriptif dengan teknik wawancara semi terstruktur, observasi serta analisis dokumen dari wakil kepala sekolah bidang kurikulum, guru akuntansi, serta pengelola perpustakaan. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan adanya dampak positif seperti meningkatnya partisipasi murid, pemahaman konsep yang lebih baik, dan keterampilan praktis yang relevan dengan kebutuhan industri. Namun, masih terdapat beberapa tantangan yang menghambat proses implementasi, seperti perubahan kebijakan yang terlalu cepat, kurangnya bahan ajar yang memadai, kesiapan guru, serta kurangnya sarana pendukung seperti buku ajar terkini. Untuk memastikan implementasi berjalan optimal, diperlukan peningkatan kompetensi guru, penyediaan perangkat ajar yang lengkap, konsistensi kebijakan, serta kolaborasi sekolah dan perpustakaan untuk efektivitas yang berkelanjutan. The infectious disease (ID) specialist is a clinician who manages patients with bacterial, viral, fungal or parasitic infections, particularly the most complex, difficult-to-treat or emerging ones. Although most ID specialists consider their added value self-evident, this view is not universally shared, and the supporting evidence deserves wider recognition. This review summarizes the literature on the relevance and impact of the specialty in the hospital setting. Published studies suggest that ID consultation improves the diagnostic work-up, the appropriateness of antimicrobial therapy and the management of community-acquired, nosocomial and complex infections, with the timing of the intervention and continuous involvement in patient care appearing decisive. We also describe the competencies that define the specialty (transversality, organizational capacity and the role of anti-infective referent) and the recent developments reshaping its practice, including infection prevention and control, telemedicine, rapid diagnostics, nanomaterials and artificial intelligence. This synthesis is of particular relevance in Morocco, where the specialty has been established in the civilian sector for about two decades but remains nascent within the military health service.

Focusing on the core characteristics of water disaster scenes-extreme environments，rapid situational evolution，information sparsity，cascading risks，and spatial concealment-this study elucidates the essential connotations of water disasters and their on-site environments. Based on a generalized full-chain cognitive paradigm，a four-layer theoretical framework for thorough perception，"sensing-cognition-integration-feedback"，is constructed. It involves four core technical pathways: multi-dimensional resilient sensing，intelligent fusion cognition，digital twin simulation，and precise collaborative feedback. The scientific issues underlying water disaster scenarios caused by naturally-driven and human factors are systematically examined. The two types of scenarios are distinguished by their respective technical emphases on "speed" and "depth". Three common key scientific and technological bottlenecks identified are information acquisition and transmission under extreme conditions，deep fusion of physics-based mechanisms with data-driven approaches，and real-time closed-loop regulation of complex systems. This framework achieves a full-cycle value transformation from data collection to operational action，providing systematic theoretical support for full-element，multiscale perception and rapid emergency response in water disaster scenarios.

This chapter employs computer-mediated communication as a thematic lens to illuminate how transnational migrants navigate connectivity and agency within digital environments. We focus on relational communication engaged in by transnational migrants, especially for unprivileged ones, thereby uncovering the intersecting dynamics that shape their experiences of social inclusion and exclusion. Here, “relation” extends beyond mere migrant-media interactions but encompasses: (1) transnational social connections; (2) digital hybridity within networks; and (3) negotiated identities bridging cultures. Though continuously impacted by technological and geopolitical shifts, migrants negotiate the tensions of displacement, constructing agency across diverse digital media. Future scholarship should critically address the escalating influence of non-human agents that fundamentally reshape these relational dynamics, particularly generative artificial intelligence.

Background: The workplace represents an ideal setting for cardiometabolic prevention, enabling early identification of workers with overweight and metabolic alterations and the implementation of structured lifestyle interventions. In this context, collaboration between the occupational physician and the dietitian integrates risk assessment with a personalized nutritional pathway, aimed at improving adherence to the Mediterranean diet and daily habits. Case presentation: Within a workplace health promotion study conducted in a university hospital in Rome, two clinical cases are described. The first patient, a 65-year-old woman with overweight, abdominal obesity, impaired fasting glucose, and low adherence to the Mediterranean diet, showed at three-month follow-up a reduction in body weight from 78 to 75 kg, waist circumference from 99 to 97 cm, normalization of blood glucose, and improved dietary and physical activity habits. The second patient, a 61-year-old man with hypercholesterolemia and impaired fasting glucose, initially presented with a weight of 86.7 kg and a waist circumference of 97.5 cm; after three months, weight decreased to 81.5 kg and waist circumference to 93.5 cm, with normalization of altered metabolic parameters. Results: In both cases, the most relevant outcome was a substantial shift in dietary habits toward a Mediterranean pattern, associated with an overall improvement in lifestyle, with benefits in both anthropometric and metabolic parameters. Conclusion: These cases suggest that an integrated pathway combining occupational health surveillance and nutritional counseling, embedded within workplace health services, may represent an effective, sustainable, and reproducible approach for preventing non-communicable chronic diseases, strengthening the role of the workplace as a key setting for health promotion.

The Flexible Image Transport System (FITS) is a widely adopted standard for storing, exchanging, and analysing astronomical data. Developed in 1979, formally described in 1981, and endorsed by the International Astronomical Union in 1982, FITS combines multidimensional numerical arrays and tabular data with structured metadata that support scientific interpretation. This narrative review examines the historical development and internal architecture of FITS, including Header/Data Units, data types, and header keywords relevant to photometric calibration, coordinate transformations, and observational provenance. It compares FITS with consumer and general-purpose raster formats, distinguishing the preservation of numerical values from the retention of astronomical metadata and calibration context. Representative applications in major space missions and observatory pipelines illustrate the role of FITS in managing images, spectra, and time-series data. The review also discusses the preparation of FITS-based data for artificial intelligence and machine learning, including calibration, quality filtering, normalization, and metadata integration. Particular attention is given to the distinction between archival data containers and the numerical arrays or tensors used by computational models. FITS provides a well-established foundation for reproducible astronomical analysis, although scientific validity and model performance depend on data quality, calibration, preprocessing, and methodological choices rather than file format alone. The review offers an educational foundation for students and researchers developing computational methods for astronomical classification and physical parameter estimation.

documents.abstract: Abstract The rapid advancement of Financial Technology (FinTech) has significantly transformed the structure and functioning of the Indian financial system. The growth of digital payment platforms, mobile banking, artificial intelligence (AI), cloud computing and data-driven financial services has changed the way individuals and businesses access and use financial services. In India, digital payments have emerged as an important component of financial transformation, while Artificial Intelligence is increasingly being used for fraud detection, credit assessment, customer service, risk management and personalised financial services.This study examines the role of FinTech in transforming the Indian financial system, with particular emphasis on digital payments and Artificial Intelligence. The study proposes an analytical framework linking FinTech adoption, digital payment usage, AI-enabled financial services, consumer trust, cybersecurity and financial inclusion. A structured questionnaire can be used to collect primary data from users of digital financial services. The proposed study may employ descriptive statistics, correlation and regression analysis to examine relationships among the major variables. The paper also discusses opportunities and challenges associated with technology-driven financial transformation, including cybersecurity risks, digital fraud, data privacy, technological barriers and the digital divide.

Abstract Artificial Intelligence, also known as AI, is transforming the modern workplace by making employees more efficient at analyzing, creating, admin and decision making. Modern AI systems have the capability of handling vast amounts of data, identifying patterns, creating content, summarizing information, offering recommendations, and conversing in natural language. These capabilities are driving organizations to adopt a model where technology and employees work together rather than the traditional automation model. But, human-AI collaboration doesn't just happen by simply introducing an AI tool. It relies on employee capability, trust, transparency, organizational preparedness, governance of data, security of privacy, and defined humans' role. This paper explores the concept of human–AI collaboration and its impact on productivity, decision-making, creativity, learning, customer service, and organizational performance. It creates a conceptual framework that unfolds around five related dimensions: AI capability, human capability, interaction and trust, organizational readiness, and responsible AI governance. The paper also evaluates the challenges that include job transformation, algorithmic bias, lack of explainability, privacy and security concerns, skill deficits, change resistance, and overreliance on AI. A human-in-the-loop approach is suggested, to enable the level of human involvement to correspond to the risk of the task. The paper argues that the best model for the workplace is not one that pits man against machine, but one that uses AI to drive computational power and leaves judgment, creativity, context, ethics, interpersonal responsibility, and accountability to the humans. The activity encompassed discussions on AI's role in decision-making, its impact on productivity, the future of work, responsible AI, and the skills required to work alongside AI.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence has really transformed areas like healthcare, legal services, education, finance, and business. But its quick spread also brings persistent tech troubles, mainly the confusing issue of AI mistakes, errors, and misinformation. Large Language Models (LLMs) can handle all sorts of tasks, from text creation and code writing to answering questions and summarizing info. Still, despite their big achievements, LLMs sometimes spout incorrect stuff – factually wrong or made-up content – which is called "hallucination." This paper dives deep into AI failures, showing how they differ based on errors in logic, generated fiction presented confidently, and correct data being misinterpreted. It looks at why AI systems act overly sure of themselves, how messy training data messes up, and ideas for fixing this like boosted retrieval methods, cleaner training data, and humans checking the work. What stands out is that these glitches aren't just random tech snafus. Instead, they're a design quirk of big AI language models. Fixing them demands teamwork from folks in various fields, not just developers. So, while there are big issues, figuring out ways to collaborate could make these systems way more reliable in the future.

documents.abstract: Abstract Academic libraries are undergoing a profound paradigm shift, evolving from passive hybrid repositories into autonomous, AI-augmented knowledge ecosystems. While traditional hybrid frameworks address basic print-digital coexistence, they suffer from critical vulnerabilities: high-demand resource friction, physical material mutilation, licensing piracy, unauthorized access, and algorithmic bias in digital discovery. This paper introduces a novel operational paradigm—the Zero-Trust Anti-Deviance Architecture (ZT-ADA)—that integrates Generative AI, Predictive Anomaly Detection, and Dynamic Resource Orchestration (DRO). Under ZT-ADA, predictive models anticipate resource surges during peak evaluation cycles, pre-allocating dynamic multi-user digital access and personalized generative summaries to mitigate physical collection stress. Simultaneously, a zero-trust cyber-physical verification matrix continuously evaluates access telemetry to detect physical deviance (mutilation, concealment, retention abuse) and digital breach threats in real time. We present mathematical formulations, operational workflows, risk matrices, and empirical evaluation metrics to establish a resilient, ethical, and scalable blueprint for 21st-century academic libraries.
topics: Library Collection Development and Digital Resources

documents.abstract: Abstract Physiotherapy is moving from an episodic, clinic-centred model of care towards a continuous, data-informed and patient-centred model. Wearable technologies, which include inertial measurement units, surface electromyography sensors, smart textiles, photoplethysmography-based devices, pressure-sensing insoles and smart garments, now capture movement, muscle activity, physiological load and adherence data outside the clinic. When these data streams are interpreted by artificial intelligence (AI), including machine learning and deep learning, they can be transformed into clinically meaningful information such as exercise quality, gait deviations, fall risk, fatigue, pain-related behaviour and recovery trajectories. This manuscript reviews the technological foundations of AI-guided wearables, describes their utility across musculoskeletal, neurological, cardiopulmonary, sports, geriatric and paediatric physiotherapy, and explains how they fit within a smart healthcare ecosystem built on the Internet of Medical Things, cloud analytics and tele-rehabilitation. The potential benefits include objective assessment, personalised dosing of exercise, improved adherence, remote supervision, early detection of deterioration and wider access to rehabilitation, particularly for under-served populations. The paper also examines the principal limitations: sensor validity, algorithmic bias, data privacy, regulatory uncertainty, cost, digital literacy and the risk of de-skilling. A five-layer implementation framework and a set of recommendations for clinicians, educators, researchers and policy makers are proposed. It is concluded that AI-guided wearables should be positioned as decision-support tools that extend, and never replace, the clinical reasoning and therapeutic relationship at the centre of physiotherapy practice.
