documents.abstract: This paper explores the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in legal research and judicial decision support. It examines the key technologies currently in use, the tangible benefits they offer (such as efficiency, cost reduction, and improved access to justice), and the critical risks that have emerged in practice (including algorithmic bias, opacity, automation bias, and confidentiality concerns). Furthermore, the paper proposes institutional governance measures and responsible workflows to ensure that AI innovation remains aligned with the core principles of the rule of law, including competence, candor, fairness, and reasoned decision-making. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Legal Tech, Judicial Decision Support, AI Ethics, Algorithmic Bias, Legal Research, AI Governance, Open Access
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as one of the most influential technologies shaping modern marketing. The rapid growth of digital platforms, customer data, and automated technologies has changed how businesses understand consumers, communicate with audiences, and measure marketing performance. AI enables organizations to analyse large datasets, predict consumer behaviour, personalize communication, automate routine tasks, and generate content. This research paper examines the role of AI in marketing, its major applications, benefits, challenges, ethical concerns, and future implications. The paper argues that AI can significantly improve marketing effectiveness when combined with human creativity, strategic judgment, and responsible data practices. At the same time, concerns regarding privacy, algorithmic bias, misinformation, transparency, and employment demonstrate the need for careful and ethical implementation. The future of marketing is therefore likely to depend on a collaborative relationship between human marketers and intelligent technologies.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become one of the most influential technologies shaping software engineering in recent years. This transformation has moved beyond early code generation and completion tools toward systems capable of participating in requirements analysis, design, testing, debugging, documentation, and solving complex software problems. The aim of this review paper is to examine the evolving role of AI in software engineering, with a particular focus on the transition from code generation tools to reasoning-based infrastructures. In this study, relevant research and studies on the application of Large Language Models (LLMs), code generation tools, and intelligent systems across different phases of the software development lifecycle are reviewed and categorized. The distinction between automatic code generation and capabilities such as problem analysis, planning, multi-step reasoning, and solution evaluation is also discussed. Findings from the reviewed literature indicate that AI can evolve from an auxiliary tool for generating code fragments into an effective factor in supporting more complex software engineering processes. However, issues such as output correctness, reasoning errors, code security, dependence on training data, trustworthiness, and the necessity of human oversight remain significant challenges in this field. Finally, the paper emphasizes the need to move from a purely "code generation" perspective toward a more comprehensive approach based on human–AI collaboration in software engineering processes.

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly becoming part of the environments in which religious questions are explored, and values are interpreted and transmitted across generations. Although existing scholarship addresses digital religion and the ethical and educational implications of AI, the mechanisms through which conversational AI may influence intergenerational religious communication within families require further conceptual examination. This article develops a Responsible Relational AI Mediation Model grounded in family pedagogy, religious socialization theory, digital religion studies, AI ethics, and Catholic personalist anthropology. This study employs an interdisciplinary conceptual approach based on critical literature analysis and synthesis, supplemented by selected international policy documents and Catholic Church teaching. The proposed model integrates three analytical dimensions: structural, identifying the persons, relationships, communities, and technologies involved in religious formation; processual, examining how AI-generated interpretations may influence perceived authority and intergenerational dialogue; and normative, establishing criteria for responsible technological mediation. It distinguishes between relationally integrated and non-integrated pathways of AI-mediated religious inquiry and recognizes generative AI as an educational tool, a mediator of interpretation, and a potential environment for ongoing religious learning. This article argues that the formative significance of AI depends on how its use is connected with critical discernment, interpersonal relationships, and religious community participation. The model offers a conceptual framework for future empirical research rather than establishing causal effects of AI on religious formation.

Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in nursing management through workforce modelling, quality surveillance, resource allocation and organisational decision support. However, artificial intelligence leadership in nursing management remains conceptually underdeveloped, particularly regarding governance, accountability and nursing-specific leadership responsibilities. Objective: To analyse and define artificial intelligence leadership in nursing management and develop a conceptual framework for future empirical research, competency development and responsible AI implementation. Design: A concept analysis using Walker and Avant’s eight-step methodology, supported by a structured search to identify conceptually relevant interdisciplinary literature. Setting: Peer-reviewed interdisciplinary literature and authoritative policy and professional guidance documents identified through PubMed, Google Scholar, Europe PMC, ProQuest Nursing & Allied Health Database and relevant authoritative sources, published between 2020 and 2025. Main outcome measures: Defining attributes, antecedents, consequences, model cases and empirical referents. Results: Twenty-four substantive sources were retained for conceptual analysis; methodological and theoretical foundations were used separately to guide analysis and support theoretical positioning. Artificial intelligence leadership in nursing management was conceptualised as a governance-specialised extension of nursing leadership comprising five interrelated attributes: strategic AI direction-setting, managerial AI literacy, ethical and regulatory oversight, organisational change leadership and workforce capability development, and systematic integration into nursing management processes. Antecedents were organised as core or contextual conditions; consequences were differentiated into proximal and proposed distal consequences, the latter requiring empirical validation. Empirical referents were identified at individual, workforce and organisational levels. Conclusions: Artificial intelligence leadership in nursing management clarifies the leadership responsibilities required when AI informs nursing managerial decision-making, including algorithmic accountability, human oversight and preservation of professional nursing judgement. The concept provides a foundation for competency development, empirical validation and organisational governance across health and aged care settings, including Asia-Pacific contexts.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly supports financial decision-making, risk assessment, service innovation, and customer interaction. This study maps the Web of Science (WoS) -indexed literature on AI technologies in financial services and financial technology (FinTech) through a PRISMA-guided bibliometric analysis of 512 English-language articles published from 2016 to 2025. Performance analysis, VOSviewer co-word mapping, CiteSpace timeline analysis, and keyword burst detection are combined to examine publication patterns, research contributors, thematic structure, and changes in scholarly attention. The selected corpus shows rapid publication growth and three prominent co-word domains: AI-driven FinTech innovation, machine learning for credit risk and fraud detection, and user adoption of digital financial services. Temporal mapping and the recent burst of the keyword 'trust' indicate increasing scholarly interest in governance-related and user-oriented concerns, alongside established technical applications. These trends also highlight the relevance of environmental, social, and governance (ESG) considerations, particularly AI sustainability, financial inclusion, and responsible governance. Drawing on these observed patterns, the study advances a socio-technical interpretation in which trustworthy AI governance is proposed as a conceptual linkage among innovation, risk management, and user adoption. The framework is an interpretive synthesis, not an empirically validated causal model. Because the study uses a predefined WoS-only search without formal cross-database or search-strategy sensitivity testing, the findings apply to the selected corpus and should not be regarded as exhaustive of the global literature. The resulting research agenda emphasises responsible management of information resources in AI-enabled financial services.

Objectives: The effective prevention and control of cervical cancer (CC) depend on high-quality screening. However, traditional cytology interpretation faces challenges such as strong subjectivity, significant inter-observer variability, and a shortage of cytopathologists in primary care settings. The distribution of high-quality medical resources in China is highly uneven between urban and rural areas. Artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted cytology offers a new approach to enhance screening efficacy. This study evaluated the diagnostic performance of a deep learning-based AI-assisted cytology system in a multicenter clinical environment in China, comparing its utility as a standalone tool and in a collaborative model with cytopathologists. Materials and Methods: This was a multicenter, crossover study enrolling a total of 769 outpatient liquid-based cytology samples obtained from three participating hospitals. Using a crossover design, two junior-to-mid-level cytopathologists from primary hospitals performed independent diagnoses and AI-assisted diagnoses (following an AI preliminary screening combined with cytopathologist verification), which were compared with AI-alone diagnoses. Using an expert cytology panel diagnosis as the cytological reference standard, sensitivity (Se), specificity (Sp), overall accuracy, positive predictive value (PPV) negative predictive value, and false-positive rates/false-negative rates and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) were calculated and compared for each modality at the atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance (ASC-US+), low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (LSIL+), and high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (HSIL+) thresholds. Results: The study found that the independent diagnostic Se of the primary cytopathologists was insufficient (LSIL+: 46.0% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.359–0.564)–50.6% (95% CI: 0.403–0.608); HSIL+: 36.6% (95% CI: 0.236–0.519)–46.3% (95% CI: 0.321–0.613), indicating a high risk of missed diagnoses. AI-alone diagnosis showed high Se (ASC-US+: 92.9% [95% CI: 0.877–0.960]) but a relatively lower PPV (72.0% [95% CI: 0.654–0.778]). AI-assisted diagnostic model achieved a favorable balance. Across all diagnostic thresholds, the AI-assisted modality significantly outperformed cytopathologist-alone diagnosis. At the ASC-US+ threshold, AI-alone Se was 92.9% (95% CI: 0.877–0.960) with a Sp of 90.9% (95% CI: 0.883–0.929), whereas the sensitivities of the two primary cytopathologists alone were 68.4% (95% CI: 0.607–0.752) and 81.3% (95% CI: 0.744–0.866), respectively. With AI assistance, primary cytopathologist Se increased to 92.3% (95% CI: 0.870–0.955)–94.2% (95% CI: 0.893–0.969), and Sp reached 94.6% (95% CI: 0.925–0.961)–96.9% (95% CI: 0.952–0.980). At the LSIL+ and HSIL+ thresholds, where cytopathologist-alone sensitivities were low (LSIL+: 46.0% [95% CI: 0.359–0.564]–50.6% [95% CI: 0.403–0.608]; HSIL+: 36.6% [95% CI: 0.236–0.519]–46.3% [95% CI: 0.321–0.613]), AI assistance improved them to 80.5% (95% CI: 0.709–0.874) and 73.2% (95% CI: 0.581–0.843)–75.6% (95% CI: 0.607–0.862), respectively, with Sp exceeding 97.0% in both cases. Receiver operating characteristic curve analysis confirmed that the AUC for AI-assisted diagnosis (0.938 [95% CI: 0.911–0.965]–0.971 [95% CI: 0.946–0.996]) was significantly higher than that for cytopathologist-alone diagnosis (0.791 [95% CI: 0.746–0.836]–0.868 [95% CI: 0.819–0.918]). Conclusion: In this exploratory study, the AI-assisted cytology system may help reduce the experience gap for primary cytopathologists in primary hospitals, substantially improving the Se and Sp of cervical cytology interpretation. The AI-assisted diagnostic model is an effective strategy for achieving standardized, high-quality CC screening, particularly for promoting homogeneous services in regions with uneven healthcare resources.

documents.abstract: Abstract Equitable digital education is central to Sustainable Development Goal 4 (SDG 4). Yet as digital systems shape how education is delivered, assessed and governed, a deeper divide is emerging between countries that can merely adopt educational technologies and those that can develop, adapt and govern them. This study examines the global distribution of technology-shaping capacity in education using 274,825 educational-technology patent records filed from 2006 to 2025. We combine four-period spatial mapping, concentration measures, 16 technology themes, annual trajectories, and LightGBM-SHAP interpretation of high-value patents from 2013 to 2023. Geographic participation expanded after 2011, yet inventive activity remained strongly concentrated: the leading country accounted for 63.48–77.62% of records across the three mature periods, while the five leading countries consistently exceeded 90%. Innovation shifted from stand-alone teaching tools toward virtual reality, artificial intelligence, adaptive learning, platform-based services and data-intensive systems. Geographic, technological and temporal variables contributed 33.33%, 27.03% and 25.78%, respectively, to the prediction of high-value patents, and high-value inventions were concentrated in a limited set of country-theme pathways. These patterns reveal a capability divide overlooked by connectivity indicators. Education systems may gain access to advanced tools without gaining the capacity to adapt them to local languages and curricula, audit algorithms, govern data or develop alternatives. By revealing where technology-shaping capacity and high-value innovation are concentrated, this study can help policymakers identify priorities for capability building, technology transfer and governance support to advance more inclusive and sustainable digital transformation toward SDG 4.

Abstract Objective:Accurate interpretation of planar ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) scintigraphy, used for diagnosing pulmonary embolism (PE) based on PIOPED/EANM guidelines, requires objective assessment of mismatched V/Q defects. Manual delineation of V/Q defects is time-consuming, subject to interobserver variability, and rarely performed in practice, limiting standardized reporting and quantification of disease burden. To address these challenges, we evaluated four modern AI models for automated segmentation of vascular perfusion defects in planar V/Q scans and compared their performance to human annotators.Approach:We retrospectively identified 2,118 patients who underwent planar V/Q scans at The Ottawa Hospital (June 2019-February 2023). Six standard projections (ANT, POST, LAO, RAO, LPO, RPO) were included. Four 2D neural networks (U-Net, nnU-Net, Swin UNETR, and a Bottleneck Transformer U-Net [BTU-Net]) were trained on 1,313 patients (7,878 projections) and validated on 329 (1,974 projections) using physician-annotated defects. A hold-out test set of 46 high probability patients was used to evaluate segmentation quality, and defect detection accuracy using free-response receiver operating characteristic (FROC) analysis.Main results:BTU-Net was the only model performing on par with human readers, showing robust sensitivity across the entire range of segmentation probabilities. At 1.5 false positives per projection rate (FPPR), BTU-Net outperformed other models with sensitivity of 0.529 ± 0.026, On a separate hold-out set of low likelihood of disease patients (n=430), the lowest FPPR was 0.08 ± 0.01 for BTU-Net (P<0.0001).Significance:BTU-Net enables rapid, consistent, and accurate interpretation of planar V/Q scans. Such tools may enhance diagnostic efficiency, standardize reporting, and support non-expert readers in evaluating PE.

documents.abstract: Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) remains the cornerstone of revascularization in coronary artery disease. However, despite advances in stent technology, adverse outcomes related to suboptimal stent placement including under-expansion, malapposition, incomplete coverage, edge dissection, and neoatherosclerosis persist. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) is the highest resolution widely available intravascular imaging modality, allowing unparalleled visualization of stent-vessel interactions and plaque morphology. However, there are significant barriers to large-scale OCT adoption, including time-consuming manual interpretation and dependence on the operator, resulting in significant variability between analysts. Artificial intelligence (AI)-based automated OCT analysis promises to assist PCI by delivering rapid, reproducible, and standardized stent optimization, but current analysis systems lack important features to optimize stent placement. This review summarizes the principles of OCT in PCI, the evidence for OCT-guided optimization, and recent advances in AI-driven automated OCT analysis. We discuss plaque analysis and classification, highlighting how AI-driven automated OCT analysis can identify fibrous, lipid-rich, and calcified lesions and guide tailored lesion preparation using balloons, specialty balloons, drug-coated balloons, intravascular lithotripsy, and atherectomy. We outline emerging AI-enabled workflows for fully automated PCI optimization, evaluate clinical outcomes, interpretability, and workflow integration. Finally, we explore future directions including AI imaging-physiology fusion, multiomics integration, and robotics. If successful, automated AI-empowered OCT analysis could become a central imaging platform for precision PCI, enabling tailored lesion preparation, optimal stent deployment, and improved clinical outcomes in coronary artery disease management.

documents.abstract: Abstract: Health-related social needs such as housing instability, food insecurity, and transportation barriers are associated with worse health outcomes and increased health care utilization, particularly among older adults. Although health systems increasingly screen for these needs, many lack the capacity to provide follow-up support at scale. This pilot evaluation described the implementation and early operational performance of an artificial intelligence-supported, on-demand patient navigation service integrated into an urban safety-net health system. From July 2024 to March 2025, providers placed 149 referrals from family medicine and geriatrics clinics. Outreach was attempted for all referred patients, and successful contact occurred for 78 patients. Navigators submitted 301 applications for public benefits and community resources; 145 were approved, while others remained pending or in process at analysis. Program costs during the observation period were approximately $5,000. These findings suggest feasibility while highlighting the need for further evaluation of patient experience and outcomes.
topics: Food Security and Health in Diverse Populations

documents.abstract: Attention to students' emotional dimension represents a key determinant of both academic success and future personal and social development (Weber et al., 2016). Within this perspective, the design of emotionally meaningful learning experiences, including those supported by Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based conversational technologies, can enhance students' well-being and engagement by recognizing emotions as a fundamental component of learning processes. Through Natural Language Processing techniques and affective computing models, intelligent conversational systems can detect and interpret users' emotional states and dynamically adapt interactions accordingly. In particular, so-called empathic conversational agents (Ortega-Ochoa et al., 2024) are artificial entities designed to elicit empathic responses from users (Hall & Woods, 2006) and to generate highly personalized simulated environments by modulating content, feedback, and task difficulty according to identified emotional factors. Such artificial conversations enable learners to engage in adaptive learning experiences in which their emotional state becomes an active variable in the regulation of the educational pathway. Chapter in: Francesco Peluso Cassese (ed.), Algorithmic Heartbeats: Affective Education in the Age of the Fourth Revolution, REN Press – Cares srl, 2026, pp. 116-117. ISBN 979-12-82860-00-0. Volume DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23211262. Section: Hybrid and "Emotionally Aware" Learning Environments.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (AI) offers scalable feedback on student writing; however, its effects on writing performance and motivation relative to teacher feedback remain insufficiently understood. Drawing on Feedback Intervention Theory and Self-Determination Theory, this study examined the comparative effectiveness of AI-generated and teacher-provided feedback on students’ writing performance and motivational outcomes. Methods A randomized controlled study assigned 312 undergraduate students to one of three conditions: AI-generated feedback, teacher feedback, or a control condition without substantive feedback. A total of 287 participants were included in the analyses. The study evaluated revised-essay quality, feedback engagement, writing self-efficacy, intrinsic motivation, perceived relatedness to the feedback source, and AI literacy. Results Both AI-generated feedback and teacher feedback produced higher revised-essay quality than the control condition, with effect sizes of d = 0.60 and d = 0.59, respectively. The two feedback conditions were statistically equivalent within a prespecified equivalence margin of ±0.35 standard deviations. Feedback engagement, but not writing self-efficacy, statistically accounted for the observed performance advantage. Teacher feedback elicited higher intrinsic motivation than AI-generated feedback, although AI-generated feedback also yielded higher intrinsic motivation than the control condition. This motivational difference was associated with perceived relatedness to the feedback source. The indirect effects identified in the analyses are associational rather than causal. AI literacy did not significantly moderate the effect of feedback on writing performance ( p = 0.058). Discussion Within the context of a single feedback-and-revision cycle at one institution, the findings suggest that AI-generated feedback can achieve writing-performance outcomes comparable to those of teacher feedback, while providing weaker motivational support. These results highlight the potential value of blended feedback approaches that combine the scalability of AI-generated feedback with the relational and motivational strengths of teacher–student interaction. Further research across multiple institutions and repeated feedback cycles is needed to establish the generalizability and longer-term implications of these findings.

The integration of artificial intelligence is generating rapid transformations in society and, particularly, in higher education institutions. Its incorporation offers significant opportunities for teaching and learning processes, but it also raises challenges related to academic integrity, privacy, bias, authorship, equity, plagiarism, and the generation of false information. This reflective essay aims to analyze the main ethical aspects associated with the use of artificial intelligence in higher education institutions and to highlight the responsibilities of the different actors within the educational community. Methodologically, the study adopted a qualitative, documentary, and reflective approach based on the critical analysis of recent scientific literature and documents from international organizations addressing ethics and the use of artificial intelligence in educational contexts. The analysis highlights the need to establish clear institutional policies, regulations, and guidelines that promote the ethical, transparent, and responsible use of these technologies. It is concluded that higher education institutions play a fundamental role in regulating their use, educating students and faculty, and promoting continuous ethical reflection to ensure that technological innovation is aligned with academic integrity, the protection of rights, and human responsibility.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: RESUMO O assédio moral constitui forma de violência psicológica capaz de degradar o ambiente de trabalho, comprometer a saúde do trabalhador e afetar a eficiência institucional. Nas Polícias Militares e nos Corpos de Bombeiros Militares estaduais, a análise do fenômeno exige especial cautela, porque o exercício legítimo da autoridade convive com estruturas rígidas de hierarquia e disciplina. Este artigo examina os elementos caracterizadores do assédio moral, suas formas de manifestação e suas consequências, distinguindo-o do poder regular de comando, fiscalização e correção. Adota-se pesquisa qualitativa, bibliográfica e documental, com análise da Constituição Federal, da Lei nº 6.880/1980, da Lei nº 14.751/2023, do Código Penal Militar, de proposições legislativas e de literatura especializada. Sustenta-se que hierarquia e disciplina não autorizam humilhação, perseguição, discriminação ou desvio de finalidade. Embora ainda não exista tipo penal federal específico e vigente de assédio moral no Código Penal Militar, o fato pode produzir responsabilização civil, administrativa e, conforme as circunstâncias, penal. Conclui-se que a prevenção depende de liderança ética, canais protegidos de denúncia, apuração imparcial, proteção contra retaliações, formação continuada e acompanhamento da saúde ocupacional, sem enfraquecimento dos fundamentos constitucionais das instituições militares. Palavras-chave: assédio moral; militares estaduais; hierarquia; disciplina; abuso de poder; saúde ocupacional. ABSTRACT Workplace bullying is a form of psychological violence capable of degrading the work environment, harming workers' health and impairing institutional effectiveness. In State Military Police and State Military Fire Brigades, its assessment requires particular caution because legitimate authority operates within rigid structures of hierarchy and discipline. This article examines the defining elements, manifestations and consequences of workplace bullying, distinguishing it from lawful command, supervision and correction. It adopts a qualitative, bibliographic and documentary approach based on the Federal Constitution, Federal Laws No. 6,880/1980 and No. 14,751/2023, the Military Criminal Code, legislative proposals and specialized literature. The study argues that hierarchy and discipline do not authorize humiliation, persecution, discrimination or misuse of authority. Although no specific and effective federal criminal offense of workplace bullying currently exists in the Military Criminal Code, abusive conduct may result in civil, administrative and, depending on the circumstances, criminal liability. Prevention requires ethical leadership, protected reporting channels, impartial investigations, safeguards against retaliation, continuing education and occupational health monitoring, without weakening the constitutional foundations of military institutions. Keywords: workplace bullying; state military personnel; hierarchy; discipline; abuse of authority; occupational health.

This article argues that AI-governed systems, and large language models in particular, introduce a novel dynamic into contemporary figurations: one of asymmetric dependency, in which people are materially, and increasingly affectively, dependent upon systems that are not, in turn, affectively dependent upon them. This condition attenuates the affectively reciprocal interdependency on which psychogenetic processes depend in Norbert Elias’s account of the civilising process and gives rise to what we distinguish as behavioural civilising: the shaping of observable conduct through monitored compliance rather than through the internalisation of restraint. Because such systems simulate human exchange whilst stripping it of its negative social consequences, they simultaneously suspend the shame functions through which figurational pressure is ordinarily converted into self-restraint and so exert decivilising pressures within the same figuration. Extended engagement with conversational AI also introduces generative reflection: a mode of exchange in which thought is elaborated and transformed rather than merely returned. We thereby extend the Eliasian framework whilst specifying the conditions under which psychogenetic processes are disrupted and transformed.

documents.abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into educational contexts is profoundly transforming teaching and learning processes, creating new opportunities for personalized instruction while simultaneously raising pedagogical, ethical, and professional challenges (Chen et al., 2020; ZawackiRichter et al., 2019). While traditional technology acceptance models have primarily emphasized the role of digital competencies and perceived usefulness (Davis, 1989; Venkatesh et al., 2003), more recent studies suggest that AI adoption is also shaped by emotional factors, including anxiety, distrust, fears of professional replacement, and concerns about the quality of the educational relationship (Schepman & Rodway, 2020; Liu & Liu, 2025). Within this framework, the present study investigates the combined contribution of cognitive and emotional factors to the development of attitudes toward Artificial Intelligence, assuming that AI acceptance is a multidimensional process in which knowledge, competencies, and emotional experiences interact dynamically. Chapter in: Francesco Peluso Cassese (ed.), Algorithmic Heartbeats: Affective Education in the Age of the Fourth Revolution, REN Press – Cares srl, 2026, pp. 319-320. ISBN 979-12-82860-00-0. Volume DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23211262. Section: Teacher Education Between the "Frankenstein Complex" and the D-Generation.

documents.abstract: Purpose – This study examines how artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the external audit, focusing on three linked outcomes: audit quality, auditors' professional skepticism, and the competences auditors need. Design/methodology/approach – An integrative literature review of 18 peer-reviewed studies in accounting, auditing and information systems published between 2016 and 2026, complemented by recent standard-setting documents from the IAASB and the PCAOB. Studies are coded by AI application, audit phase, research method and outcome, and synthesised thematically. Findings – AI extends audit coverage from samples to full populations and improves anomaly detection, fraud prediction, the evaluation of estimates and the efficiency of routine procedures. Archival evidence links AI investment by audit firms to fewer restatements, lower fees and more accurate going-concern and internal control opinions. However, the benefits depend on the human–machine relationship: auditors may discount AI evidence (algorithm aversion) or accept it without sufficient challenge (automation bias), and both can impair judgment. Model opacity, data quality, accountability and limited guidance in auditing standards remain unresolved risks, although standard setters have begun to respond. Research limitations – The review is integrative rather than systematic, covers English-language studies only and relies mainly on evidence from the United States, Europe and large audit firms. Evidence on generative AI in auditing is still at an early stage. Implications – Audit firms should treat AI output as evidence to be evaluated, design workflows that prompt challenge and protect the development of junior staff. Standard setters should clarify how much assurance AI-based procedures provide, and educators should combine data analytics with judgment training. Originality – The review integrates technical, behavioural and institutional strands into a single framework in which AI is proposed to affect audit quality mainly through calibrated professional skepticism and auditor competence. It derives five testable propositions and a research agenda relevant to both developed and emerging audit markets.

The authenticity of Islamic Religious Education in elementary schools faces significant contemporary challenges, shifting from transformative character building toward mechanical cognitive memorization. This study aims to re-actualize the core principles of authentic moral learning through a mindful, meaningful, and joyful paradigm tailored for elementary school students. Using a literature study approach with critical-qualitative analysis, this research examines classical and contemporary pedagogical frameworks to synthesize an integrated moral education model. The findings indicate that mindful learning enhances students' self-awareness and spiritual presence, meaningful learning connects religious doctrines with daily life experiences, and joyful learning fosters intrinsic motivation and emotional well-being. Synthesizing these three elements restores the authenticity of IRE, transforming moral learning from rigid doctrinal instruction into a living, transformative spiritual and ethical experience.

Drones that can fly around on their own in groups are really good at watching things, helping with disasters, and doing work in factories. They have a hard time working together, scaling up, and changing what they do when things get complicated. When one person or computer is in charge of all the drones, it takes too long to make decisions. When the drones make their decisions, they have a hard time not running into each other and saving energy. So, we made a way for drones to work together using artificial intelligence. This way uses various kinds of learning and lets the drones make their own decisions. We tried this way with computers, and it worked really well. The drones got better at working, did things faster, finished tasks, and did not run into each other as much, even when there were a lot of things in their way.
